name: Evaluative Binominal
pattern: NP[... Nom₁ of NP₂], with Nom₁ predicated of the referent of NP₂

entry.name: Evaluative Binominal
entry.pattern: NP[... Nom₁ of NP₂], with Nom₁ predicated of the referent of NP₂

1.definition: Evaluates the person or thing introduced by the second nominal.
1.details: A nitwit of a husband evaluates the husband as a nitwit. Material and measure expressions such as a statue of bronze and a cup of water supply different relations. The usual singular oblique takes a(n). Kim and Sells document bare plural obliques. The evaluation can apply to a complex first nominal, as when destroyer of education is predicated of the minister. That semantic grouping leaves the attachment of the outer PP open.

examples.note: The husband is the target of the evaluation.
BNC example with a bare plural oblique.

examples.form: [that destroyer of education of a minister]
examples.note: Published judgment. Education is what the minister destroys.

relatedConstructions.notes: The whole expression can serve as an NP.

grounds.note: Reports bare plural obliques and argues for a constructional analysis.

projection.target: The first nominal supplies a description of the referent contributed by the second. A bare plural second nominal can support that relation.
projection.evidence: CGEL's clausal paraphrase and the published singular and plural cases investigated by Kim and Sells.

curious.title: A noun of a noun, used to judge
curious.summary: In a phrase like a nitwit of a husband, the first noun is a judgment about the person or thing named by the second.
curious.body:
In her stupid nitwit of a husband, the husband is the target of the evaluation. The first noun, nitwit, is said of the husband. This is different from a statue of bronze or a cup of water, where of expresses a material or a measure.

The first part can be bigger than one word. In that destroyer of education of a minister, the education is what the minister destroys, and destroyer of education is the judgment passed on the minister.

examples.text: [that destroyer of education of a minister]

curious.try: Think of a judgment you could pass on a person with a noun, then fit it into a phrase of that shape.

teacher.summary: Helps explain evaluative noun of noun phrases, and how they differ from material and measure of-phrases.
teacher.explain: In an evaluative binominal, the first nominal is predicated of the referent of the second: a nitwit of a husband evaluates the husband as a nitwit. Material and measure expressions such as a statue of bronze and a cup of water supply different relations. This dictionary notes that the usual singular oblique takes a(n) and that Kim and Sells document bare plural obliques (wobbly jellies of men). The evaluation can apply to a complex first nominal, as in destroyer of education of a minister, where education is what the minister destroys; that grouping leaves the attachment of the outer PP open.
teacher.terms: This dictionary calls the judging use an evaluative binominal.

examples.text: [that destroyer of education of a minister]

contrasts.note: The first noun evaluates the husband.

watch_for: A learner might read a nitwit of a husband as two people, a nitwit and a husband.
A learner might read of in a statue of bronze as evaluating, when it gives a material.
teacher.activity: Students sort phrases with of (a nitwit of a husband, a cup of water, a statue of bronze) by whether of expresses a judgment, a material or a measure.
